relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: The rescued child becomes a forty-year king, while his mother's name remains in the record.
Joash's right action is tied to the years in which Jehoiada teaches him.
Public devotion continues outside the centralized sanctuary.
Many kinds of sacred giving enter one institution.
The original plan trusts priests to gather funds and repair visible damage.
Twenty-three years expose a system that received money without completing its purpose.
The king asks the neglected question: why are the breaches still open?
The priests relinquish both collection and construction responsibility.
A simple chest creates a visible path for public gifts.
Royal and priestly officers count the growing fund together.
Money moves from treasury into hands supervising actual work.
Wood, stone, craft, transport, and labor close the building's wounds.
The repair fund is protected from decorative expansion.
Resources are spent on workers and structural need.
Faithful supervisors are trusted, though trust never needs to become secrecy.
Other offering income remains with the priests.
Hazael's conquest turns toward Jerusalem.
Sacred and royal wealth become tribute to purchase the city's reprieve.
The royal archive holds what this account leaves outside the frame.
Servants turn palace access into conspiracy.
The once-hidden child king dies by hands inside his own house, and succession continues.

contemplative_note: The chapter moves from repair to extortion and assassination. Its clearest wisdom is structural: good intention is not enough when money disappears into an ineffective system. Breaches close when funds become transparent, workers are trusted and paid, and beauty yields to actual repair. Yet even a restored sanctuary cannot protect a kingdom that remains trapped in imperial pressure and palace violence.
